Stephen of Obazine
STEE-vun uv oh-bah-ZEEN
n. (c. 1085–1159, Limousin hermit and founder of Obazine, affiliated to Cîteaux in 1147)
Stephen, from Greek stephanos, a crown; Obazine, a place name of the Corrèze.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Stephen was a priest of the Limousin who about 1124 went with a companion into the forest of Obazine to live as a hermit. Others came, as they always did; he built, organised, and found himself governing a community of men and, nearby, a house of women, which was unusual and which he refused to abandon. In 1147 he brought the whole foundation under Cîteaux, and Obazine became a Cistercian abbey with its sister house of Coyroux still in its care. He was a builder of roads and bridges as well as of cloisters, and the aqueduct his monks cut into the cliff face still carries water. This dictionary records Stephen because his career answers a question the solitary life always raises: what happens when the hermit is found? Scripture's answer is that he is not permitted to stay hidden, because a city on a hill cannot be, “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14). The gift he was given was for others, “minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1Pe 4:10), and the care he would not drop is what pure religion is said to look like, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27), “Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a hermit as a solitary living in seclusion; a founder as one who establishes; to minister as to serve or supply; a burden as that which is borne with labour; and a steward as one who manages for another.

expand to see more

HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret; a beadsman.

FOUNDER, n. One that founds, establishes and erects; one that begins, or lays a foundation; one from whom any thing originates.

MINISTER, v.t. To give; to afford; to supply; to serve in any office or duty; to attend and serve.

BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; that which is grievous, wearisome or oppressive.

STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and receive and pay money.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:14 — "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid."

1Pe 4:10 — "As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God."

Jam 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Gal 6:2 — "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

Modern Corruption

Limousin hermit turned abbot, c. 1085–1159: found in his forest, he built roads, an aqueduct and a house of women he refused to abandon.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the solitary who is discovered is not thereby interrupted; he is assigned. Stephen went to the forest for himself and spent thirty-five years on other people, which is the normal course. Scripture states the impossibility of staying hidden when God intends otherwise, “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14), and makes every gift a trust held for others, “As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another” (1Pe 4:10).

The second thing is his refusal to drop the women's house. Affiliating to Cîteaux would have been simpler without Coyroux, and the order was reluctant; he kept it. Pure religion in James is defined by exactly that kind of inconvenient care, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27), and the law of Christ is fulfilled by carrying what is not yours to carry, “Bear ye one another's burdens” (Gal 6:2).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek polis (G4172), a city; Greek charisma (G5486), a gift of grace; Greek oikonomos (G3623), a steward; Greek threskeia (G2356), religion; Greek baros (G922), a weight.

expand to see more

Greek polis (G4172) — a city, set where it must be seen; “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid”, Matthew 5:14.

Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace, held in trust; “as good stewards of the manifold grace of God”, 1 Peter 4:10.

Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a household steward; “minister the same one to another”, 1 Peter 4:10.

Greek threskeia (G2356) — outward religious service; “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction”, James 1:27.

Greek baros (G922) — a weight, a load borne for another; “Bear ye one another's burdens”, Galatians 6:2.

Usage

"“A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14) — the hermit who could not stay hidden."

"“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27) — the house he would not give up."

"“Bear ye one another's burdens” (Gal 6:2) — the law he was actually keeping."
